title: Septic System Urgency Assessment
intro: Nine questions about what the system is actually doing right now. The result is an urgency classification, what it means, and what to do next — no contact details required to see it.
disclaimer: This assessment is a triage tool built on the standard warning signs, not a diagnosis. Only an on-site inspection with the tank open can confirm what is happening underground. If sewage is entering the building, treat it as an emergency regardless of what this says.

questions.text: Is sewage currently backing up into the house — a floor drain, a tub, or the lowest toilet?

options.label: It has in the last week

questions.text: Is there standing effluent, or wet and spongy ground, over the drain field?
How many drains in the house are running slowly?
Is there a sewage odour indoors, or near the tank or field outside?

options.label: Outdoors, near the tank or field

questions.text: Do toilets gurgle, or does water rise in a toilet when a washing machine drains?
When was the tank last pumped?

options.label: Never, or no record at all

questions.text: How does the household size compare to the tank?

options.label: 4+ people on a 1,000-gallon tank or smaller
Not sure of the tank size

questions.text: Is there a pump tank or aerobic unit, and is its alarm sounding?

options.label: There is a pump or aerobic unit, no alarm

questions.text: Do the symptoms appear only after sustained rain?

options.label: Yes — fine in dry weather, bad when wet

results.headline: Treat this as an emergency
results.meaning: The answers describe an active failure: sewage where it should not be, or a system that has stopped accepting water. Raw sewage carries bacteria and pathogens, and every additional gallon of water used makes the situation worse.
next: Stop using water completely — no flushing, laundry, dishwasher or showers.
Keep people and pets away from any affected area, indoors or out.
Do not open the tank lid. Septic tank gases displace oxygen and have killed people who leaned in.
Call now for priority dispatch — the tank is pumped down first, then the cause is diagnosed.

results.headline: Book service within days, not months
results.meaning: The system is showing multiple stress signals at once. This pattern usually means the tank is full or a component has failed, and it typically becomes a backup rather than resolving on its own.
next: Reduce water use — spread laundry out, delay anything that can wait.
Book a pump-out with inspection so the cause is identified, not just the symptom relieved.
If sewage appears indoors or in the yard before the appointment, treat it as an emergency and call.
Note when symptoms started and whether they track with rainfall — it changes the diagnosis.

results.headline: Due for service — schedule it on your own timeline
results.meaning: The answers point to a system approaching its interval or showing early signals, without an active failure. This is the point at which pumping is straightforward maintenance rather than damage control.
next: Schedule a pump-out in the next few weeks rather than waiting for symptoms.
Ask for baffle condition and sludge depth to be recorded so the next interval is a date rather than a guess.
If there is no service record for the property, ask for a documented inspection alongside the pump-out.
Check nothing is parked or stored on the drain field footprint.

results.headline: No urgent signals — keep to the interval
results.meaning: Nothing here suggests an active problem. Septic systems fail quietly, so the interval matters more than symptoms: by the time signs appear, solids have often already been reaching the drain field.
next: Keep to a 3–5 year pumping interval, shorter for a large household on a small tank.
Have sludge depth recorded at the next service so the interval becomes specific to this system.
Keep vehicles, sheds and pools off the drain field footprint.
Keep wipes, grease and solvents out of the system — the short list that causes most avoidable failures.
